part1-imports.desc: Verifies that a file's imports only point: - Sideways (to siblings in its own module); or - Deeper (into nested modules) And that they never point (violations): - Up to a parent module; or - Across into a different branch of the tree
part1-imports.exception: Imports to a common module (see below section). If a common module is at `crate::app::[common]`, any files at or below `crate::app` may import it.
part1-imports.rationale: To keep a predictable module tree structure, where we know everything in a module's submodules are supporting logic for the module to call, and not the other way around (i.e. where submodules call up to their parent modules for supporting logic).

more-details.detail: Sideways/deeper imports must be written with `super::...` (i.e. never `crate::...`).
Imports to a common module (which isn't a sibling) must be written with `crate::...` (i.e. never `super::super...`).
more-details.rationale: To make the code more readable by distinguishing between a sideways/deeper import and an import up and 1 over to a common module.

common-modules.desc: These are modules for shared code. The following are their names and what they are for: - c: free-functions - t: types - s: `static` items - cnst: `const` items - ext_traits: extension trait definition and implementations Each may be a folder (e.g. `t/`) with a mod.rs file, or a single-file module (e.g. `t.rs`)
common-modules.example: - `crate::c` is the whole-crate shared free-functions, reachable everywhere
common-modules.note: Inside a common folder, the imports must still be sideways or deeper (i.e. `c/foo/bar.rs` cannot import `c/util.rs`, which sits above it, just because they are both in `c/`). A common folder re-roots the tree: inside it, the same up/across prohibitions apply, but measured from the common folder rather than the crate.
common-modules.rationale: There must be a way to share certain items between separate modules that have different submodules, because otherwise it would be impossible to write DRY code. In fact, this might be exaggerating it, but it would maybe even be impossible to write code at all. So, if we didn't have these common modules, the import rules would be too strict to work.

part2-item-homes.desc: Verifies that the following top-level items are only defined as public in the following common modules: - `static`: `s` - `const`: `cnst` - `struct`, `enum`, and `type` alias: `t` - `trait`: `t` and `ext_traits`
part2-item-homes.rationale: We want consistent locations for all user defined items

part3-common-publics.desc: Verifies that the public surface (i.e. leaf items reachable from outside the module) in the following common modules is limited to the following items: - `s`: `static` - `cnst`: `const` - `t`: `struct`, `enum`, `type` alias, and `trait` - `ext_traits`: `trait` - `c`: `fn`
part3-common-publics.rationale: We want consistent items on the public surface of common modules

part4-common-nesting.desc: Verifies that no common modules are nested in other common modules.
part4-common-nesting.rationale: Make reasoning about common modules easier

exception.desc: A common module may be nested inside another common module of the same kind (e.g. `/c/foo/c/bar`, `/t/foo/t/bar`). There may be as much nesting of these as desired.
exception.rationale: It's commonly necessary to nest a common module to share code within a common module of that same kind.

part5-impl-locations.desc: Verifies that all impls: - Live in a `t` common module; and - Are in the same file or a sibling file of the type's definition.
part5-impl-locations.exceptions: - For foreign types (i.e. not defined in our crate; like: `impl SomeTrait for Vec<T>`), the impl must live in an `ext_traits` common module. - For private types, impls in the same file as the type definition are allowed. - If we are implementing a foreign trait (i.e. `impl ForeignTrait for MyType`), it is allowed anywhere.
part5-impl-locations.rationale: To have an expected location for impls. Also to gently encourage small impls, preferring free-functions over methods.

part6-c-fn-location.desc: Verifies, for each function on the public surface of a c module sitting at [D]/c, that the nearest common ancestor (NCA) of its call-site modules is [D] itself.
part6-c-fn-location.rationale: We want functions in c modules at the right level of the tree.
part6-c-fn-location.note: We won't worry about a similar rule for other common module types (e.g. `t`). Those users can specify those other items where they want.

config.item: ignore_export_macros - when true, imports of macros that use `#[macro_export]` are exempt (default false)
